ARMORED RESCUE VEHICLE (BEARCAT) 
LPD is in dire need of a new armored rescue vehicle (BearCat) that provides its 
occupants and officers responding on foot, using the vehicle as a moving shield with 
ballistic protection beyond what is provided by ballistic shields, helmets, and vests, 
offering greater safety to community members and officers during high-risk incidents. 
Leading up to the October 25th mass shooting, LPD’s only armored vehicle (an 
MRAP) was out of service due to significant mechanical breakdowns that far exceeded 
what could be absorbed by the department’s annual budget. Before, during, and in the 
months after the October 25th mass shooting, the men and women of LPD continue to 
be at a disadvantage in high-risk situations without the protection afforded by an 
armored rescue vehicle.    
A BearCat is also considerably smaller than LPD’s current out-of-commission 
armored rescue vehicle, which will provide greater mobility in tight city streets. It’s most 
commonly used for rescuing persons whose lives are placed in extreme danger by being 
otherwise trapped in a life-threatening situation where either all-terrain and/or 
defensive armament is required.  This armored rescue vehicle will be integrated into 
other departmental trainings, including firearms, COBRA/HAZMAT, active shooter, and 
hostage rescue trainings.  
In the past, the old LPD armored rescue vehicle has been an invaluable tool that 
has been proven effective, primarily in the response for rescuing persons whose lives are 
placed in extreme danger by being otherwise trapped in a life-threatening situation 
where either all-terrain and/or defensive armament is required. During the October 
25th mass shooting, and in countless other incidents since our current armored rescue 
vehicle has been out of service, the men and women of LPD continue to be at a 
disadvantage in vulnerable situations without the protection afforded by this type of 
vehicle. This vehicle also plays a vital role in our capability to promote dialogue and 
negotiation in high-risk scenarios.

The question. The Committee's April recommendation said in-kind contributions could make up 
"some or all the requested amount" (Item 6855 p. 6). Public statements reported on October 31 
(Sun Journal) made a fair point: many owners already contribute substantially in other ways. 
Section 7 answers it by letting credit cover the whole Suggested Contribution, but only for 
services that relieve the City, and an Agreement may direct an owner's money to needs the City 
names (5.7). 
Credit and directed money (7.2, 5.7). Two separate things. Credit lowers the amount 
suggested. Directing money to a need, through an Agreement, does not change the amount; it 
decides where the money goes. 
• City services: a service the City, its schools, General Assistance or emergency medical 
service provides or funds, which the owner provides mainly for Lewiston residents. It is 
valued at the lesser of the owner's cost and what the City or schools spend on the same 
service (7.5), so credit approximates what the City saves. For example, if an owner pays for a 
nurse to work two days a week in a Lewiston public school, its credit is whichever is lower: 
what the nurse costs the owner, or what the schools would have paid for the same nurse. 
• Directed money for listed needs: an Agreement may direct an owner's contributions to 
needs on a list the Council adopts each year on the Committee's recommendation, drawn 
from the budget: services reduced or requests not funded (5.7, 7.3). The Council approves the 
first year's appropriation with the Agreement and later years' in each year's budget. Directed 
money is cash, not credit: it does not lower the Suggested Contribution. Contributions 
outside an Agreement reduce the levy (6.4). In FY2027, for example, the schools eliminated 
26 full-time positions (Item 6868 p. 6), and the adopted budget reduced the Recreation 
request from $887,081 to $733,261 and did not fund a requested Public Health Coordinator 
(Item 6787). 
What does not. An owner's own teaching, training or required operations, including course 
requirements, internships and clinical training (7.4.1); unpaid volunteer time (7.5; the owner's 
own cost of staffing and running a program still counts under 7.5(a)); general economic effects; 
billed care; and services offered to everyone as part of ordinary operations (7.4). An owner may 
report all of its other community work, and the annual report lists it, in the owner's words, if the 
owner asks (7.8). That work is recognized, but it does not change the amount. 
Why this design. Programs elsewhere credit services that reach residents and that the city would 
otherwise fund (Boston Task Force report, 2010; file 20044 pp. 263–264). Where the rules were 
looser, credit grew and cash did not: in Boston most owners claim the full 50% credit allowed, 
and cash payments have changed little in a decade (Boston FY2025 recap). Studies of service-
learning measure benefits to students well and to communities less (Tryon & Stoecker 2008; 
Blouin & Perry 2009), which is the reason for 7.4.1. Standard hourly rates for volunteer time 
overstate its value to the people served (Brown 1999), which is why credit uses cost. Valuing 
services at what the City itself spends keeps credit to what the City saves and makes it checkable 
against the budget.

Choices for the Committee. 
• Tax relief or services. Contributions outside an Agreement reduce the levy (6.4); money an 
Agreement directs to a listed need adds a service instead (5.7). The Council weighs that 
choice in each Agreement vote. An owner's board can approve a multi-year grant to a named 
public need more readily than a payment to reduce taxes, so most cash is likely to come 
through Agreements directed to listed needs; the Committee should expect levy relief mainly 
from Agreements that choose it. 
• Positions. Money that adds or restores a position comes only through an Agreement of at 
least [three] years with [one year's] notice before it ends (7.3), so the City is not left with a 
cost when payments stop. 
• Owner-run programs count only if the Council credits them when approving an Agreement 
(7.6), in public. The same exclusions (7.4) and valuation (7.5) apply, so this route cannot 
credit teaching or value a service above what the City would spend. The bracketed words 
would limit it to services new or expanded under the Agreement, so that the route pays for 
something new rather than relabeling work an owner already does; existing services that save 
the City money still earn ordinary credit under 7.2. 
• Other community work. Because credit counts only City-type services, an owner could 
shift money away from uncredited work, such as grants to local nonprofits, or claim work it 
already does. Documented cuts are rare: a 2004 Worcester report states that Brown 
University eliminated more than $600,000 of support for a community health and education 
program to fund its Providence payment (Worcester Regional Research Bureau, "Will 
PILOTs Fly in Worcester?", Report 04-04, p. 7). Relabeling existing work is the more 
common effect elsewhere, which is why 7.2 to 7.6 are narrow. Recent agreements in New 
Haven and Ithaca state that the institution's existing community programs continue "over and 
above" the payment (Yale News, Nov. 17, 2021; Cornell Chronicle, 2023); an Agreement 
here could say the same, and 7.8 lists other community work publicly each year.

for Lewiston students, free use of facilities and Council priorities, valued at the owner's cost, 
with credit up to [50]%; (b) section 7 with a [50]% or [75]% cap; (c) counting all community 
benefit an owner reports. Option (c) answers the concern most fully, but it would likely bring
